# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Descriptive hypothesis: Teriflunomide promotes myeloid differentiation in differentiation-arrested acute myeloid leukemia through on-target dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibition

In acute myeloid leukemia with a block to myeloid maturation and continued dependence on de novo pyrimidine synthesis, teriflunomide is hypothesized to induce differentiation by inhibiting dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH). The primary endpoint is acquisition of mature myeloid features and reduced leukemic propagation at exposures that preserve a colony-forming reserve in normal hematopoietic progenitors. Bulk viability, leukemia-stem-cell function, and cytarabine-residual disease are scored as separate endpoints. Unverified prior knowledge, requiring verification against regulatory labeling: teriflunomide is approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis, and leflunomide, approved for rheumatoid arthritis, is a prodrug of teriflunomide.

Supported premises are confined to the packet. DHODH inhibition promotes myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affects disease-related endpoints in the models investigated, connecting nucleotide metabolism to a differentiation outcome that is distinct from nonspecific cell killing [S4]. Whether an approved drug that affects this pathway reproduces that result at a selective exposure is unresolved by [S4]. Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the specimens studied often had low reactive oxygen species and elevated BCL-2, and BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells [S1]. Those data support a selectivity question; they leave an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor without an established therapeutic window [S1]. In cytarabine-treated models, residual cells were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells. They showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related oxidative metabolism, and altering that state changed treatment response in the settings studied [S2]. Venetoclax with azacitidine is an established comparator that engages TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation changes in leukemia stem cells [S3]. Here that regimen is only a mechanistic control, because the proposed drug, original indication, and primary endpoint differ.

Speculative bridges are labeled as assumptions. Teriflunomide is assumed to phenocopy DHODH inhibition as characterized in [S4]. Compound identity in that study is unspecified here, and the packet contains no teriflunomide experiment. Differentiation-arrested blasts are assumed to depend more on de novo pyrimidine synthesis than normal CD34-positive progenitors, which would open a window; differences in nucleotide salvage sit outside [S1]-[S4]. The same differentiation response is assumed to appear in ROS-low leukemia stem cells [S1] and in cytarabine-residual oxidative cells [S2]. Anti-inflammatory or kinase activities sometimes discussed for this pharmacologic class are unverified prior knowledge.

Alternative explanations are built into the test. Clearance of blasts may represent nucleotide starvation and nonspecific cytotoxicity. Benefit may instead track disruption of the oxidative residual-cell state [S2] or the BCL-2-high, ROS-low vulnerability already linked to venetoclax-based therapy [S1], [S3]. Off-target pharmacology may shift surface markers with DHODH remaining inactive.

The discriminating preclinical strategy uses primary AML samples that retain a differentiation block in short-term culture, matched comparison with healthy-donor CD34-positive cells, a ROS-low stem-cell assay aligned with the population in [S1], and a cytarabine-residual assay aligned with [S2]. Teriflunomide is titrated around documented human plasma exposure. Those exposure values are unverified prior knowledge and require confirmation before concentrations are fixed. A chemically distinct DHODH inhibitor provides the on-pathway comparator. Uridine supplementation is the rescue condition, on the unverified prior-knowledge premise that extracellular uridine bypasses DHODH through salvage. Prespecified readouts stay separated: myeloid morphology together with CD11b and CD14 acquisition at preserved viability (differentiation); annexin V positivity and colony loss without maturation (bulk killing); engraftment in an immunodeficient mouse (stem-cell function); and colony formation by healthy CD34-positive cells (normal-cell window). Dihydroorotate accumulation or a pyrimidine-pool change documents pathway engagement. Venetoclax with azacitidine is included only to measure whether oxidative-phosphorylation suppression of the kind reported in [S3] also follows teriflunomide.

A falsifying observation is any of the following at DHODH-engaging concentrations inside documented human exposure: differentiation markers remain unchanged in differentiation-arrested AML; uridine fails to reverse anti-leukemic activity; a second DHODH inhibitor is inactive, or activity occurs without pyrimidine-pathway engagement; or concentrations that mature AML blasts suppress normal progenitor colonies to the same degree, leaving no selectivity window. Reduction in blast number without maturation falsifies the differentiation hypothesis.

Limitations are substantial. [S4] supplies experimental evidence about DHODH inhibition, while clinical efficacy, protein binding, and marrow free-drug concentrations of teriflunomide remain outside the packet. The stem-cell state in [S1] and the cytarabine-residual state in [S2] are different populations, so a bulk differentiation response leaves clearance of either population unshown. Variable salvage capacity can remove the window. Unverified prior knowledge: labeling for the multiple-sclerosis indication includes serious hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity warnings, which would still constrain translation after a positive laboratory result. Randomized comparative efficacy is outside the scope of this hypothesis.

Ranked proposal:
Teriflunomide promotes myeloid differentiation in differentiation-arrested acute myeloid leukemia through on-target dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibition
